title: Band Keratopathy: The Calcific Bridge
summary: A chronic corneal degeneration characterized by the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite in the subepithelial space, Bowman's layer, and anterior stroma. This textbook-grade guide covers its metabolic, inflammatory, and surgical management pathways.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Band Keratopathy (BK) is a chronic, degenerative condition involving the deposition of grey-to-white calcium hydroxyapatite crystals in the anterior cornea. Deposits typically begin at the peripheral 3 and 9 o'clock positions, separated from the limbus by a 'lucid interval' of clear cornea, eventually progressing centrally to form a horizontal band across the interpalpebral fissure.

branches: Evaporation of tears increases local pH
Loss of CO2 at the interpalpebral fissure
Primary site: Bowman's Layer & Subepithelial space

rows: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) - most common in kids, Chronic Uveitis, Phthisis Bulbi, Interstitial Keratitis.
Hypercalcemia, Hyperphosphatemia, Chronic Renal Failure, Hyperparathyroidism, Sarcoidosis, Vitamin D Toxicity, Milk-Alkali Syndrome.
Chronic exposure to Mercury (preservatives), Silicone Oil in the Anterior Chamber, Phosphate-containing eye drops.
Primary calcific band keratopathy (rare), Familial forms.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Peripheral inception at 3 and 9 o'clock limbus.
Lucid Interval: A clear zone between the limbus and the calcium deposit (due to lack of Bowman's layer at the extreme periphery).
'Swiss Cheese' appearance: Small holes in the band representing where corneal nerves pierce the Bowman’s layer.
Surface irregularity: Leading to foreign body sensation and secondary epithelial erosions.
Advanced progression: Centripetal growth across the visual axis leading to vision loss.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Laboratory Panels
content: Step 1: Serum Calcium and Phosphate levels (rule out hyperparathyroidism/renal issues).
Step 2: Serum Albumin (to calculate corrected calcium).
Step 3: BUN and Creatinine (assess renal function).
Step 4: Serum ACE and Chest X-ray (if sarcoidosis suspected).
Step 5: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) levels.

sections.title: Surgical Management: EDTA Chelation
content: 1. Anesthesia: Topical Proparacaine/Tetracaine +/- peribulbar block for long cases.
2. Epithelial Debridement: Use a #15 Bard-Parker blade or alcohol (20%) to remove epithelium overlying the calcium.
3. Chemical Chelation: Apply Disodium EDTA (1.5% to 4%) using a cellulose sponge or a well (e.g., a 6-8mm trephine ring).
4. Mechanical Scraping: Use a blade or diamond burr as the calcium softens/dissolves.
5. Irrigation: Copious rinsing with Balanced Salt Solution (BSS) to remove residual EDTA and debris.
6. Post-Op: Bandage Contact Lens (BCL), topical antibiotics, and NSAIDs/Steroids.

rows: White/Yellow line at 3/9 o'clock; no clear lucid interval.
Amber-colored oily droplets; collagenous, not calcific.
Lipid deposition; involves the entire circumference; has lucid interval.

content.explanation: C: Chronic Uveitis; A: Age-related/Alkali (Milk-Alkali); L: Local (Silicone oil); C: Chronic Renal Failure; I: Increased Serum Ca2+; U: Under-treated Sarcoidosis; M: Mercury exposure.

sections.title: Advanced Treatment Options
content: PTK (Phototherapeutic Keratectomy): Excimer laser ablation for smoother surface but risks hyperopic shift.
Diamond Burr Polishing: Often combined with EDTA for faster results.
Amniotic Membrane Grafting: For persistent epithelial defects post-chelation.
Lamellar Keratoplasty: Reserved for cases with deep stromal involvement.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: When to worry
content: Bilateral BK in a child: High suspicion for Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA).
Rapidly progressive BK: Likely systemic hypercalcemia or renal crisis.
Stromal Melting: Can occur if EDTA is used for excessive durations or high concentrations.
Non-healing epithelial defect post-op: Risk of secondary infection/keratitis.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Recurrence: High risk if the underlying cause (e.g., uveitis, hypercalcemia) is not controlled.
Induced Astigmatism: Resulting from irregular corneal surface.
Hyperopic Shift: Especially after deep scraping or PTK laser treatment.
Prognosis: Generally excellent for vision if the visual axis is cleared and the macula is healthy.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the 'Lucid Interval'; its presence is hallmark for BK vs. Arcus/Limbal Girdle.
EDTA 0.05M (1.5% to 3.0%) is the standard concentration; higher concentrations risk toxicity.
The 'Swiss Cheese' holes are technically called 'Nerve Canals of Bowman’s Layer'.
Silicone oil-induced BK is more common in aphakic eyes where oil contacts the corneal endothelium.

sections.title: Landmark Insights: Phosphate-Free Drops
sections.content: Recent studies and the AAO BCSC emphasize avoiding phosphate-buffered eye drops (e.g., certain Prednisolone or Dexamethasone formulations) in patients with corneal surface compromise, as they can accelerate the precipitation of calcium phosphate on the cornea, worsening BK.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations: JIA Focus
content: JIA is the most common systemic association in children.
BK may be the presenting sign of asymptomatic uveitis.
Requires collaborative care with Pediatric Rheumatology.
Aggressive treatment of the underlying uveitis is mandatory to prevent recurrence.
